query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of Hf to a eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve both room-temperature yield strength and tensile ductility by promoting the formation of Hf‐rich precipitates that reinforce the internal lamellar interfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase (FCC/B2 or equivalent) lamellar colonies that display microcracking along internal boundaries and limited tensile ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, trace addition of Hf (e.g., approximately 0.5 atomic percent) into the alloy composition prior to casting.
generation.conditions: Alloy casting and standard thermomechanical processing to retain the lamellar colony microstructure, with room-temperature tensile testing and microstructural characterization.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of Hf-rich precipitates that segregate to the phase and grain boundaries within the lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: The Hf-rich precipitates pin the boundaries and inhibit the nucleation and propagation of microcracks, thereby reducing localized stress concentrations. Simultaneously, these precipitates provide precipitation strengthening within the hard phase (e.g., B2), resulting in net improvements in both yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony alloy, the Hf-modified alloy will exhibit an increase in yield strength and a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature tensile ductility (higher plastic strain before failure) due to enhanced interface stability and crack arrest mechanisms.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy that shows high strength when processed conventionally but suffers from brittle fracture initiation due to microcracks along the numerous internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when Hf is added in trace amounts (around 0.5 atomic percent) and when processing conditions allow for its proper segregation and precipitate formation; deviations in Hf content or processing parameters may not yield the same improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent of the strength and ductility improvement is uncertain, as it depends on the detailed morphology and distribution of the Hf-rich precipitates, which require careful microstructural analysis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy batches under identical casting and thermomechanical processing conditions—one control batch without Hf and one with a trace (~0.5 atomic percent) Hf addition. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and detailed microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM) to assess the formation and distribution of Hf-rich precipitates at phase boundaries.
measurements: Verification of Hf-rich precipitate formation and distribution (using SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-containing alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and tensile ductility compared to the control, or if microstructural analysis fails to confirm the presence of Hf-rich precipitates at the critical boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

The strengthening effect of Hf on the alloy could be maintained at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C.At different high temperatures, the Hf0.5 alloy exhibited a higher strength and ductility than the Hf0 alloys. The outstanding high-temperature strength of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the precipitation strengthening of the Hf-rich phase precipitated in the inner of the B2 phase. The excellent high-temperature ductility of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the pinning effect of the Hf-rich phase that existed at grain and phase boundaries to boundary sliding during the high-temperature deformation.
